papers.title: Deep Speech Representations Track Word Timing along a Low-Dimensional Circular Trajectory
papers.abstract: Speech timing is fundamental for speech models to recognize words accurately, but how word-timing information is represented in speech models remains underexplored. We study this question using the framework of representational geometry, which investigates whether and how concepts are represented in low-dimensional subspaces of the representation space. Prior work in cognitive neuroscience has shown that when HuBERT feature sequences are averaged across words of the same duration, they form near-circular trajectories from word onset to word offset in a two-dimensional "temporal subspace." Here we show that this circular structure of word timing is a general property of deep speech representations, by demonstrating its emergence in nine additional speech models covering both supervised and self-supervised. We then move beyond averaged word segments and show that in HuBERT, the circular trajectories are consistent enough at the level of individual words to perform word segmentation. Our approach, Rotary Segmentation (RoSeg), achieves 64.3% boundary F-score on Librispeech by detecting word boundaries when cycles complete in the temporal subspace. Although supervision is needed to identify a good subspace, nevertheless this result demonstrates much stronger implicit word knowledge in HuBERT than has previously been shown.

papers.title: D2: High-Capability Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models from Half-Duplex Backbones
papers.abstract: Full-duplex spoken language models (FD-SLMs) support simultaneous listening and speaking, but often lag behind half-duplex spoken language models (HD-SLMs) in general capabilities. We propose Dialogue-to-Duplex (D2), a framework that converts pretrained HD-SLMs into high-capability FD-SLMs at fine temporal granularity. D2 adapts the original audio encoder to streaming through decoder-free representation distillation and learns full-duplex interaction through supervised fine-tuning. We systematically study the effects of chunk size on full-duplex interaction, general capabilities, and inference computation. We apply D2 to two distinct HD-SLM architectures, Qwen3-Omni and LLaMA-Omni 2. At a 12.5Hz update rate, Qwen3-Omni-D2 achieves 99.2% turn-taking success with 521-ms latency, 99.5% interruption success, and a state-of-the-art VoiceBench score of 70.1.

papers.title: Two-Stage Multi-modal Learning for Dynamic Audio-Visual Navigation: From Physical Alignment to Scene Aggregation
papers.abstract: Embodied Audio-Visual Navigation (AVN) requires an agent to locate sound targets by jointly leveraging visual and auditory cues. While prior work has achieved notable success with static sound sources, real-world scenarios often involve moving targets, giving rise to the more challenging problem of \textbf{Dynamic Audio-Visual Navigation (D-AVN)}. Existing approaches largely rely on semantic auditory features, which limits generalization to unheard sound categories and hinders fine-grained spatial reasoning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel \textbf{Two-Stage Multi-modal Learning} framework for D-AVN. In the Physical Alignment stage, the proposed \textbf{Intensity-Calibrated Geometry Encoder (ICGE)} performs physics-informed alignment of sound intensity with visual geometry to capture category-agnostic spatial correspondence. In the Scene Aggregation stage, a Transformer-based \textbf{Cross-Modal Scene Aggregator (CMSA)} dynamically integrates multi-modal features to construct a robust state representation for policy learning. Extensive experiments on Replica and Matterport3D demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art success rates, while significantly improving generalization and navigation efficiency in complex environments and under unheard sound scenarios.

papers.title: RUBATO: Decoupled Clocks Allow Full-Duplex Models to Think as Fast as They Can
papers.abstract: Recent Speech Full-Duplex (FDX) models are capable of engaging in naturalistic conversation by listening and speaking at the same time. Building on this foundation, recent architectures introduce internal thinking streams to enhance their intelligence. To guarantee these streams process successfully in real time, existing methods enforce a fixed decoding rate, which assumes a hardware profile capable of a specific latency. We argue this static approach is severely suboptimal. Because internal thinking is intrinsically asynchronous, an ideal FDX model should sustain real-time conversational flow while allowing each stream to decode at its own hardware-adaptive rate. Thinking streams must process as fast as the hardware allows to deliver accurate answers faster. To solve this, we propose RUBATO, a novel multistream positional encoding that assigns independent clocks to entirely decouple the streams. This structural isolation empowers the model to zero-shot interpolate across any inference decoding speed. It drastically simplifies dataset construction by requiring training on only two extreme decoding speeds while smoothly adapting to any intermediate rate during deployment. RUBATO demonstrates consistent robustness across five spoken reasoning tasks. On Spoken GSM8K, a baseline model collapses to 1.7% accuracy at interpolated speeds. Conversely, RUBATO-Full sustains 48.7% to 51.1% accuracy across all rates, leveraging faster hardware to achieve a 6.5x shorter time-to-answer with a constant time-to-first-response. This advantage holds on BIG-Bench Audio and amplifies significantly during complex full-duplex interruptions. Specifically, when a user interjects while the model is actively speaking and reasoning, RUBATO-Full achieves 40.0% to 45.1% accuracy, whereas the baseline fails completely.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual TTS for Indian Languages: A Benchmark and Inference-Time Duration Estimation Strategies
papers.abstract: Recent alignment-free Text-to-Speech (TTS) models achieve high synthesis quality by removing explicit alignment modules and simplifying training. However, they often struggle in cross-lingual scenarios due to differences in character durations across languages, leading to duration mismatch and degraded speech quality. Existing approaches typically address this issue using explicit duration predictors, increasing model complexity. Systematic evaluation of TTS performance for Indian languages in cross-lingual settings remains under-explored due to the lack of standardized evaluation benchmarks. In this work, we construct a cross-lingual evaluation benchmark covering English and nine Indian languages and propose a language-aware inference-time duration estimation strategy for alignment-free TTS that incorporates language-specific duration-per character statistics without retraining or architectural modifications. We further develop heuristic formulations that refine duration estimation based on language-dependent duration variations. Experiments on bilingual and multilingual A-DMA models demonstrate improved speech naturalness, intelligibility, and speaker similarity while reducing duration mismatch.

papers.title: Word-Aligned Prosody Reflects Speaker Differences More Than Depression or PTSD Severity
papers.abstract: Word-aligned prosody is increasingly used to detect depression and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), yet the stability and clinical relevance of these measurements remain unclear. We examine stability at two levels. At the word level, we ask whether a speaker produces the same word in a similar speaker-specific way across different utterance contexts. At the speaker level, we ask whether averaging prosody across many words produces consistent speaker scores across separate recordings. Drawing on principles of psychological measurement, we compare these representations in four corpora spanning acted, spontaneous, and clinical speech. Word-specific deviations show little cross-context recurrence (0.01-0.16), whereas speaker summaries are highly consistent, reaching 0.997 in ESD, 0.73-0.90 in MSP-Podcast, and 0.84-0.996 in DAIC-WOZ and PTSD-STOP. Despite this consistency, associations with depression or PTSD severity do not exceed 0.15; equivalence tests exclude effects of 0.30 in all analyses and 0.20 in DAIC-WOZ, while within-person associations with daily PTSD symptoms are near zero ($|\rho|\leq0.04$). Thus, aggregation yields stable speaker-level prosodic measures, but these measures do not detectably track depression or PTSD severity in the studied corpora. Code is available at https://github.com/jen900704/word-aligned-prosody.

papers.title: CIViC: Evidence Gates for Audio-Conditioned Visual Prediction on Proxy Tasks
papers.abstract: Removing audio can shift a visual predictor's output without showing whether the task uses the intended audio information. We introduce Conditional Input and Visual Interpretation Checks (CIViC), a four-gate protocol that links an interpretation to an intervention, held-out task comparison, or endpoint control. We demonstrate CIViC on actor-disjoint face-raster tests, a synthetic audio-feature mixture, and source-video-disjoint SpeakerVid proxy tasks. In the static face-raster test, cross-actor audio replacement meets the registered detection rule with a small effect; on a separate temporal endpoint, constant-audio fits score better than audio-trained fits in four matched seeds. In the synthetic mixture, the condition-augmented fit has higher 1,000-step RMSE than the audio-only fit (0.1807 vs. 0.1707), with the gap shrinking during training. In the SpeakerVid proxy, the five-feature-zero fit (five low-level audio summaries zeroed; identity, dialogue, and condition inputs retained) has lower whole-frame grayscale RMSE than aligned audio across four held-out conditions and five paired seeds, while aligned audio has lower segment-drift error. The results show that output activation, held-out error, and endpoint controls support different interpretations across these proxy tasks.

papers.title: BridgeCodec: Mamba Enhanced Neural Audio Codec with Schr\"odinger Bridge at Low Bitrate
papers.abstract: Neural audio codecs achieve remarkable performance but operate as closed ecosystems with rigidly co-trained encoderdecoder pairs, severely hindering interoperability. To resolve this, we propose BridgeCodec, a versatile framework that decouples these pairs by translating latent representations between mismatched, frozen endpoints. We formulate this cross-codec translation as a Schr\"odinger Bridge optimal transport problem, enabling robust mapping between disparate distributions without predefined noise priors. To efficiently capture longrange speech temporal dependencies, we integrate a Mambaenhanced U-Net architecture. We validate BridgeCodec on an extreme deployment scenario: mapping a lightweight 8 kHz source encoder directly to a 48 kHz target decoder at an ultralow bitrate of 1 kbps. Experimental results demonstrate that BridgeCodec achieves superior wideband reconstruction and high perceptual quality, successfully bridging heavily bottlenecked, heterogeneous codecs.

papers.title: SonicWorld: Source-Centric Latent Dynamics for Spatial Audio Reasoning
papers.abstract: Dynamic spatial audio reasoning requires a model to associate changing acoustic observations with the correct source and recover its spatial state at a queried time or interval, a challenge intensified by overlapping speech and source motion. To study this problem, we introduce Sonic-Bench, comprising 2.8K first-order Ambisonics clips and 28.8K target-specific question-answer pairs across 480 simulated indoor scenes. The benchmark covers localization, distance estimation, and motion reasoning in single- and dual-source settings. We further propose SonicWorld, which integrates physical, learned acoustic, and semantic features into persistent source states through learned transitions and recurrent updates, and projects them into an Omni LLM for spatial reasoning. Compared with Spatial-Omni on the Sonic-Bench test split, SonicWorld improves direction accuracy from 31.98% to 34.69% and reduces azimuth error from 57.22{\deg} to 48.01{\deg}. In zero-shot transfer to Spatial LibriSpeech, SonicWorld retains strong localization performance, achieving 73.98% direction accuracy and 19.29{\deg} azimuth error, compared with 27.14% and 70.74{\deg} for Spatial-Omni.

papers.title: GeoMER: A Joint Euclidean-Hyperbolic Geometry Framework for Multimodal Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) aims to understand human emotions by integrating information from multiple modalities such as speech and text. Psychological studies suggest that emotions exhibit latent hierarchical structured relationships in their semantic representations. However, most MER approaches rely on Euclidean representations, which capture fine-grained cross-modal interactions but do not explicitly provide a geometric prior for organizing hierarchical emotional structures. To mitigate this gap, we propose GeoMER, a joint Euclidean-Hyperbolic modeling framework that introduces hyperbolic emotion-core routing to capture higher-level, abstract emotional representations for MER. The proposed framework jointly models token-level cross-modal semantic interactions and latent emotion representations in two complementary geometric spaces. Specifically, GeoMER consists of a Euclidean Multimodal Fusion Module (EuclFusion) for multimodal representation fusion and a Hyperbolic Geometric Core Routing (HypGeoRoute) module that performs geometry-aware core assignment and aggregation in a hyperbolic manifold to capture more abstract feature representations. The HypGeoRoute module complements the Euclidean token-level modeling. We experiment on the IEMOCAP multimodal MER benchmark and demonstrate that the proposed method achieves the best performance, with 83.54% weighted accuracy and 83.35% unweighted accuracy, outperforming Euclidean baselines, including MemoCMT.

papers.title: JSIR: An Audio-Aligned, Multi-Task Dataset of Jazz Standard Recordings
papers.abstract: Beat tracking, chord estimation, and structure analysis are staple tasks of music information retrieval. Their datasets are drawn largely from Western popular music, and jazz remains a repertoire on which state-of-the-art systems underperform. We present JSIR, the Jazz Standards dataset for Information Retrieval. Its 267 recordings of 44 jazz standards span 25.6 hours, 3.7 times the audio of JAAH, the closest existing resource. For each recording, we provide annotations for beat and downbeat positions, chords, and sections, all produced by a jazz musician and revised in several passes. In baseline experiments, models trained with JSIR also improve on other jazz datasets: the downbeat F-measure of a state-of-the-art beat tracker rises from 87.7% to 89.2%, and the seventh-chord accuracy of a pop-trained chord estimator on JAAH from 34% to 41%. We publicly release the annotations, the annotation tool used to create them, and a web application that displays them in sync with the audio.

papers.title: Explore This! Beat and Downbeat Tracking From a Learned Tatum Grid
papers.abstract: State-of-the-art beat tracking is based on neural networks that model beats and downbeats as individual events, often followed by a separate Dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN) enforcing musical consistency. We propose a novel architecture that combines deep learning with differentiable theory-based modules: Specifically, we design a system that first predicts a tatum grid, then groups tatum events to beats and downbeats, explicitly modelling multiple options for the current tempo and time signature in a bar-pointer-like fashion. Our approach improves continuity metrics compared to existing DBN-free systems and is more versatile than the de-facto standard DBN, but still falls behind the best DBN-based methods on average. Given the many design choices and hyperparameters involved, we assume we have not yet explored the full potential of this idea and publish our code and invite others to explore this further.

papers.title: LiveAnon: Improving Privacy and Utility in Streaming Speaker Anonymization with Codec Language Models
papers.abstract: Speaker anonymization (SA) aims to conceal speaker identity while preserving linguistic content and emotion, but existing streaming systems often lose emotion information through discrete content bottlenecks or require emotion-specific modeling. We present LiveAnon, a voice-conversion-based streaming SA system that directly conditions an autoregressive codec language model on hidden features from a pretrained streaming ASR encoder, preserving emotion without emotion-specific supervision. To reduce codec-generation latency, we introduce capped RVQ decoding, which preserves dependencies among coarse codebooks while predicting the remaining codebooks in parallel. Under VPC24, LiveAnon improves intelligibility and emotion preservation over fixed-target Stream-Voice-Anon (SVA), a strong prior streaming SA system, matches emotion-prompted SVA in emotion preservation, and achieves the strongest semi-informed privacy among streaming systems. Under VPC26, it ranks second across all metrics among the evaluated anonymization systems, demonstrating a strong privacy-utility balance.

papers.title: Co-Adaptive Entropy Modeling and Rate-Distortion-Optimal Bit Allocation for Perceptual Audio Coding
papers.abstract: We present a perceptual audio coder in which the entropy-coding model and the bit allocation co-adapt across blocks without model side information. Mantissas are coded by a hybrid of bit packing and arithmetic coding with per-band probability models learned online. Encoder and decoder accumulate identical histograms from decoded blocks and advance the same model state. The model enters bit allocation directly: per-band rate--distortion frontiers combine measured perceptual distortion with entropy-coded rate estimates under the current model, and a dynamic program attains the exact minimum of total objective perceptual distortion for each block's budget under the model's rate estimates, with reservoir carry-over. Under a strict per-block rate, entropy-coding-aware bit allocation lowers this distortion (band noise-to-mask ratio in linear scale) by 15-24% relative to the same solver without it, and co-adaptation removes a further 3-4% (up to 15% on oboe) that a backward-adaptive coder alone cannot realize in one pass; a MUSHRA test at 80 kbps per channel confirms the ranking.

papers.title: Phone Segmentation and Recognition through Phonological Activation Mapping
papers.abstract: Phone segmentation and recognition are inherently related tasks, yet modern approaches typically model them separately. We argue that phonetic structure is already latent in the representations of self-supervised speech models (S3Ms), so one only needs to steer them to solve both tasks. We leverage S3M-based Phonological Activation Mapping (SPAM), which maps each S3M representation frame to a vector of phonological feature activations, such as voicing and nasality. On top of SPAM, we introduce two simple but effective lightweight, gradient-descent-free prediction heads: a recognition head and a segmentation head. Our method requires less than a minute of phonetic transcriptions, and the recognition head generalizes to phones unseen during training. Across a diverse range of datasets, our approach attains strong segmentation performance.

papers.title: Why Learning Rediscovers the Closed-Form Diagonal Regularizer
papers.abstract: Recovering modal amplitudes from a few sensors requires regularization, and the shape of the penalty decides how strongly each mode is shrunk. The best shape depends on the truncation noise that discarded modes add to every measurement, which is unobserved and could be room-specific. We identify a diagonal saturation principle: for a single snapshot, isotropic truncation noise makes the Bayes-optimal Tikhonov shape a closed-form power law Gamma_k proportional to lambda_k^|s|, set by the prior alone and independent of the domain. The off-diagonal anisotropy equals the Herfindahl index H of the discarded-mode power exactly, Weyl's eigenvalue counting law fixes the number of discarded modes and hence H, and Berry's random-wave conjecture enters only through a diagonal term D, which we measure directly. Together they predict an approximately flat loss landscape over the penalty exponent, which leaves a learned diagonal regularizer little to gain from tuning the exponent per room. On simulated acoustic rooms the closed form stays within 5.83% of a per-room power-law oracle across observation windows, and three learned diagonal architectures track its error, the closest within a fraction of a point and none more than 3pp above it, while learning qualitatively different spectra. In the truncation regime no tested method consistently improves on the closed form, including Learned Iterative Ridge, which couples modes across layers. The framework extends to heat diffusion through a known Green's-function correction with no new free parameters.

papers.title: Hearing's Blind Spots: Toward Perceptual Compute Allocation in Neural Text-to-Speech
papers.abstract: A speech synthesizer produces a detailed waveform, but a listener need not hear every detail. Strong sounds can mask weaker neighbors, creating context-dependent "blind spots" in hearing. Could neural text-to-speech (TTS) spend less computation on those details? We investigate a first step: how the placement of spectral degradation affects completed speech from Piper and Kokoro. At matched time-frequency bin-removal budgets, a simple low-energy-first policy achieves higher mean wideband PESQ than random deletion and the tested psychoacoustic masking criteria. At 50% removal in the spreading-matrix comparison, energy, masking, and random policies score 4.46, 3.60, and 1.19 on Piper, and 3.42, 2.10, and 1.22 on Kokoro. Spectrograms and masking maps expose where these perturbations fall and why a model's below-threshold regions cannot automatically be treated as inaudible. Calibration diagnostics show substantial threshold sensitivity, while a small single-listener pilot establishes no transparent removal budget. CPU profiles identify waveform decoding as the main measured kernel cost, but a tested dynamic-INT8 Kokoro decoder runs slower than FP32 on both CPUs. The results establish energy ranking as a strong oracle baseline and motivate testing perceptual allocation inside a decoder. They do not yet demonstrate saved computation: the decisions here use already synthesized audio, and quality metrics are evaluated at 16 kHz. We release scripts, results, audio examples, and a listening-study instrument.

papers.title: PitchIn: Natural-Language Vocal Coaching from Unstructured Community Feedback
papers.abstract: Effective vocal coaching connects performance issues with corrective advice, but recordings paired with expert diagnoses and advice are scarce. Online singing communities provide a potential source of supervision, but observations and advice are scattered across unstructured comments. We introduce PitchIn, audio-language models for natural-language vocal coaching, and the PeerCoach Dataset: 14,445 instruction examples covering Focused QA, Overall Feedback, and Recognition QA. We compare target combinations on Qwen2.5-Omni and train PitchIn on Focused QA and Overall Feedback using Qwen2.5-Omni and MOSS-Music. On VocalCoachBench, the proportion of requested diagnosis-correction pairs matching an expert issue with valid advice rises from 21.3% to 61.0% for Qwen2.5-Omni and from 31.4% to 51.2% for MOSS-Music. Direct training on source comments yields only 19.8% for Qwen2.5-Omni. For Qwen, Focused QA alone reaches 65.6%, but adding Overall Feedback improves alignment with expert reviews and human preference. Both models improve expert-review alignment over pretrained baselines and are significantly preferred for usefulness (92.0% and 67.3%, respectively). Demo examples are available at https://hayeonbang.github.io/PitchIn.

papers.title: FAM-gate: field-aware metadata attention with prior-constrained vector gating for audio classification
papers.abstract: User-generated audio collections frequently contain textual metadata such as titles, tags, and descriptions. Effectively leveraging these complementary fields requires accounting for both field het erogeneity and varying semantic relevance relative to the acoustic content. We propose FAM-Gate, a two-stage framework for metadata-enriched audio classification. In the first stage, field-aware metadata-view attention dynamically aggregates multiple metadata views using audio-guided weighting, explicit field-identity embeddings, a shared identity-initialized projection, and mean-anchored regularized aggregation. In the second stage, a prior-constrained vector gate performs bounded, dimension-wise fusion of audio and metadata representations centered around an acoustic prior. Ex periments on BSD10K, BSD35K, and FSD50K show consistent improvements in both hierarchical single-label and multi-label classification. Compared with matched random-view scalar-fusion base lines, FAM-Gate improves the hierarchical F-score by 2.53 and 5.72 percentage points on BSD10K and BSD35K, respectively, while increasing macro mAP and macro F1 by 5.07 and 10.25 percentage points on FSD50K.

papers.title: SemiCodec: Bridging Speech Tokenization and High-fidelity Reconstruction with Semi-discrete Representations
papers.abstract: Speech representation learning requires a discrete modeling interface while preserving high waveform fidelity. Existing approaches rarely achieve both: discrete tokens ease modeling but lose fine-grained acoustic information, while continuous latents preserve fidelity but require specialized generative objectives. We introduce SemiCodec, a novel Semi-discrete neural speech Codec with synchronized discrete tokens and continuous latents. Direct joint optimization may create a reconstruction shortcut through the continuous pathway, leaving the discrete tokens insufficiently grounded. To address this issue, we propose a Preserve-then-Ground training paradigm that first establishes a high-fidelity synthesis space and then grounds SSL-guided discrete tokens within it. Experiments show that SemiCodec outperforms fully discrete codecs in reconstruction quality and intelligibility while remaining competitive with continuous representations in acoustic fidelity and speaker preservation. Audio samples are available at https://pennyw1-se.github.io/SemiCodec-Demo-Page/

papers.title: HE-NAC: High-Efficiency Neural Audio Coding via Hierarchical and Residual Multi-Band Quantization
papers.abstract: High-fidelity audio coding requires faithful reconstruction of perceptually important high-frequency components, which are often lost due to the aggressive temporal decimation and quantization of neural codecs. State-of-the-art neural audio coding methods rely on adversarial learning to hallucinate these missing components, yielding perceptually plausible but imprecise reconstructions; a limitation for high-fidelity music applications. As a remedy, we propose high-efficiency neural audio coding (HE-NAC), which provides a multi-band extension of the popular residual vector quantization (RVQ) scheme. HE-NAC introduces an effective training mechanism that harmonizes a bitrate-free blind upsampling process, residual learning to compensate it with minimal bitrate, and a multi-head decoder architecture for band-specific reconstruction. As a result, HE-NAC achieves a balanced trade-off, reliably reconstructing the core-band ($\leq$ 3 kHz) component while preserving overall sound fidelity. Subjective listening tests and objective evaluations demonstrate that HE-NAC outperforms both the DAC baseline and MPEG HE-AAC at equal or lower bitrates.

papers.title: FOAdapter: A Plug-and-Play Spatial Tokenizer for Low-Bitrate FOA Speech Coding
papers.abstract: Spatially encoded speech conveys not only linguistic information but also spatial cues. This enables listeners to distinguish and localize speakers, contributing to more natural and realistic auditory experiences in applications such as remote conferencing and immersive media. Neural speech codecs (NSCs) enable high-quality reconstruction of monaural speech at increasingly low bitrates while preserving linguistic information, but their ability to effectively preserve spatial cues remains limited. We propose FOAdapter, a plug-and-play spatial tokenizer that leverages a pretrained monaural speech codec to efficiently represent both linguistic and spatial information in first-order ambisonic (FOA) speech at low bitrates. Comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that FOAdapter consistently preserves spatial information across all evaluated codecs. Source code and audio examples are available on our demo website.

papers.title: MSVAE: Rethinking Musical Semantics in Continuous Latent Spaces
papers.abstract: Continuous latent representations underlie recent diffusion-based lyrics-to-song and text-to-music systems, yet aligning lyric conditions with these latents remains difficult: existing systems resort to generator-side machinery such as sentence-level timestamps, auxiliary alignment objectives, or semi-autoregressive decoding, while the latents they predict are still produced by autoencoders trained purely for reconstruction. We address this difficulty from the representation side. We propose MSVAE (Music Semantic Variational Autoencoder), which structures its continuous latent around two complementary semantic streams: work-level compositional content and lyric-level linguistic-vocal content. Partitioned dual-stream alignment makes both streams explicit by aligning disjoint latent subspaces with frozen lead-sheet and ASR references, while a semantic-first gated residual posterior derives its base from a frozen music-SSL encoder and admits acoustic information only through gated, bounded corrections. MSVAE achieves competitive stereo reconstruction and stronger MARBLE probing than continuous-autoencoder baselines, and improves downstream lyrics-to-song and text-to-music generation. Notably, with only an untimed phoneme prefix and no lyric timing, MSVAE yields the lowest phoneme error rate, whereas all baseline representations require sentence-level alignment to produce intelligible vocals.

papers.title: A General-Purpose Neuromorphic Sensor based on Spiketrum Algorithm: Hardware Details and Real-life Applications
papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer a biologically inspired computational paradigm, enabling energy-efficient data processing through spike-based information transmission. Despite notable advancements in hardware for SNNs, spike encoding has largely remained software-dependent, limiting efficiency. This paper addresses the need for adaptable and resource-efficient spike encoding hardware by presenting an area-optimized hardware implementation of the Spiketrum algorithm, which encodes time-varying analogue signals into spatiotemporal spike patterns. Unlike earlier performance-optimized designs, which prioritize speed, our approach focuses on reducing hardware footprint, achieving a 52% reduction in Block RAMs (BRAMs), 31% fewer Digital Signal Processing (DSP) slices, and a 6% decrease in Look-Up Tables (LUTs). The proposed implementation has been verified on an FPGA and successfully integrated into an IC using TSMC180 technology. Experimental results demonstrate the system's effectiveness in real-world applications, including sound and ECG classification. This work highlights the trade-offs between performance and resource efficiency, offering a flexible, scalable solution for neuromorphic systems in power-sensitive applications like cochlear implants and neural devices.

papers.title: SemBridge: Semantic Token Anchoring for Continuous-Latent Autoregressive Speech Generation
papers.abstract: Continuous-latent autoregressive speech generation has emerged as a promising alternative to discrete-token modeling by avoiding quantization loss and preserving richer acoustic information. However, continuous acoustic targets do not expose linguistic structure as explicit token-level prediction targets. Consequently, the autoregressive language model (LM) must acquire linguistic structure indirectly through acoustic prediction, which can compromise the content fidelity of generated speech. We propose SemBridge, a training-only semantic-token anchoring framework for continuous-latent autoregressive speech generation. SemBridge uses discrete semantic tokens to directly supervise autoregressive LM states and employs a Semantic-Aligned Acoustic VAE to organize the continuous target space under the same semantic reference. The semantic supervision is used only during training, while inference remains entirely continuous. We evaluate SemBridge on zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) and score-conditioned singing voice synthesis (SVS). Across multiple benchmarks, SemBridge improves content accuracy, as measured by word and character error rates (WER/CER), while maintaining competitive speaker similarity and perceptual quality. Experimental results demonstrate that explicit semantic-token supervision for autoregressive state learning is an effective and general direction for continuous speech generation. The model code and checkpoints will be available at https://github.com/ASLP-lab/SemBridge

papers.title: KOMOS: Automatic Mean Opinion Score Estimation for Korean Speech
papers.abstract: As speech generation and real-time spoken dialogue systems advance, neural mean opinion score (MOS) predictors are increasingly used to evaluate speech quality. However, many existing predictors are trained primarily on English read speech and generalize inconsistently across languages and speaking styles. In particular, their reliability on Korean speech has not been adequately validated. We propose KOMOS, a Korean MOS predictor for evaluating the overall quality of both read and spontaneous speech. To train and evaluate KOMOS, we collect 5,000 ratings from 29 native Korean listeners for 1,000 utterances spanning real recordings, synthesized speech, and degraded speech. KOMOS achieves an utterance-level Spearman rank correlation (SRCC) of 0.900, compared with 0.703 for UTMOS v1 and 0.767 for UTMOS v2. The inference code is publicly available at https://github.com/upskyy/komos and the trained model at https://huggingface.co/upskyy/komos.

papers.title: The NPU-ASLP System for Music Restoration in the CCF-AATC 2026 Challenge
papers.abstract: This paper presents the NPU-ASLP music restoration system developed for Track 1 of the China Computer Federation (CCF) Advanced Audio Technology Competition (AATC) 2026 Challenge. The task aims to recover clean music from mobile-device-captured recordings affected by coupled degradations from playback devices, acoustic propagation, environmental noise and recording terminals. System development is further constrained by limited and imperfectly aligned real data pairs and a strict model-complexity budget. In our system, we adopt TF-MoE as the backbone for its dual-axis modeling of cross-band and temporal dependencies, whose Top-1 routing activates a single expert per token to bound computation under the strict budget. We extend it with two task-specific adaptations: a scale-aware encoder and a complex mapping decoder. The former encodes normalized complex spectra jointly with per-band log-RMS to preserve the band-energy cues discarded by band-wise normalization. The latter directly estimates the clean complex spectrum rather than masking the input, thereby repairing coupled degradations. To address the limited, imperfectly aligned real recordings, we further build a challenge-calibrated playback--propagation--recording simulator that generates 1,572.12 h of sample-aligned data across 202 acoustic conditions. The final system contains 2.951M parameters and requires 82.659 GMACs for a 10-s input. On the official blind test, it achieved -49.067 dB SI-SNR, 1.273 LSD, 2.540 FAD, and 3.495 ViSQOL. It ranked third in LSD, FAD, and ViSQOL and received the third prize in the challenge.

papers.title: HMU-Bench: Hierarchical Music Understanding Benchmark for Omni Models
papers.abstract: Music-understanding benchmarks should identify both the evidence available to a model and the operations a correct answer requires. We introduce HMU-Bench, a bilingual benchmark with notation and audio components. ABC Q&A contains 1,029 Chinese-English question pairs across six musical domains, labeled as extraction, single-step inference, or multi-step inference. Audio Q&A contains 460 question pairs on 92 recordings, spanning five scope-difficulty configurations. All music is Suno-generated, and questions and references are human-reviewed. Reference-based evaluation of seven omni models yields high notation scores for the strongest systems, but no model averages above 1.4 on the 0-4 audio scale. Notation and audio rankings show little correlation. A transposition case study also reveals octave errors missed by LLM grading. These findings motivate separate modality reporting and event-level checks for symbolic outputs. Data, annotations, evaluator prompts, and graded responses will be released at https://github.com/stepaudiollm/hmu-bench.

papers.title: High-Fidelity Song Generation with Joint Discrete and Continuous Modeling
papers.abstract: Generating a full song from lyrics and a style description requires long-range musical planning without sacrificing vocal and instrumental detail. Low-rate discrete semantic tokens make this tractable, but quantization constrains the information available to acoustic rendering, while separately optimized stages prevent downstream generation objectives from shaping the planner. We propose joint discrete and continuous modeling for high-fidelity song generation. A VQ tokenizer supplies tokens for autoregressive planning, and a separately trained SSL-derived variational encoder supplies continuous semantic targets. Conditioned on the completed token plan and differentiable readouts of the planner's predictive states, a full-sequence flow model generates semantic features for acoustic rendering. Its flow-matching gradients reach the language model through the readouts, without differentiating through token sampling; the standard pathway keeps continuous features out of autoregressive feedback. On 192 shared prompts, its 48D configuration improves SongEval from 4.152 to 4.269 and reduces micro-PER from 20.26% to 14.47% relative to a discrete baseline, while receiving substantially higher expert listening scores. We further analyze the system through downstream semantic probes and conditioned reconstruction.

papers.title: Controllable Mono-to-Stereo Upmixing using Reward-tilted Flows
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of mono-to-stereo audio upmixing: generating a high-fidelity two-channel stereo signal from a single-channel recording. The task is fundamentally ill-posed i.e., many stereo signals are consistent with a given mono recording. An effective upmixer must therefore generate a realistic, musically coherent stereo image while preserving the underlying audio content. Previous approaches have relied on signal-processing driven decorrelation, ambience extraction and supervised learning, offering limited spatial control or requiring task-specific training. In response, we propose Aura (Audio Upmixing using Reward-tilted Flows), which reformulates upmixing as a generative inverse problem using a pretrained flow prior. To enable controllable spatial imaging, we design a reward-tilted posterior sampler whose reward penalizes divergences between generated and target distributions of inter-channel cues. Composing forward operators further enables joint restoration and upmixing without retraining or fine-tuning. Objective and subjective evaluations on real-world music recordings from MUSDB18-HQ demonstrate our method's effectiveness relative to several baselines.
